name: Lehman's Laws of Software Evolution
statement: Software that is actually used must keep changing, and grows more complex unless work is spent to fight it.
meaning: Lehman's laws of software evolution are a set of observations about how large, actively-used software systems change over time. They apply specifically to what Lehman called E-type systems, those embedded in and used in a real-world environment. The two central and most robustly supported ideas are that such a system must be continually changed or it becomes progressively less satisfactory, and that its complexity increases over time unless work is deliberately spent to reduce it. The set began as three observations around 1974 and grew to eight by the mid-1990s, empirical generalisations rather than proven laws.
mechanism: E-type software is part of the world it models, so once deployed it changes that world: users adapt, new needs emerge, and the operating environment shifts, which makes the software's assumptions drift out of date. This creates a feedback loop that forces the system to keep changing and growing to stay useful. But each change is layered onto the existing structure, so complexity rises and perceived quality falls unless effort, refactoring, re-architecting, documentation, is spent to counter it. Entropy accumulates by default, and fighting it consumes capacity that could otherwise add features, which is why maintenance dominates the cost of long-lived software.

examples.text: Lehman and Belady's original dataset was the release history of IBM's OS/360, where they measured how size, module counts, and change effort evolved release by release.

A study of the kernel over several years found it kept changing and growing, supporting the continuing-change and continuing-growth laws, but grew super-linearly, a challenge to the growth-slowdown implied by others.

Decades-old banking or enterprise systems, continually patched for new regulations, currencies, and integrations, must keep changing to remain usable while accumulating complexity that makes each change harder.

variants.name: The E, P, and S classification
variants.text: Lehman's scheme distinguishing S-type programs, judged only against a formal specification; P-type, solving a real-world problem with an approximate solution; and E-type, embedded in their environment, to which the laws apply.

variants.name: The eight laws
variants.text: Continuing change, increasing complexity, self regulation, conservation of organisational stability, conservation of familiarity, continuing growth, declining quality, and the feedback-system law, developed between the 1970s and the 1990s.

whyItMatters: The laws are the empirical backbone for how the field understands software maintenance, software rot, and technical debt: useful software cannot stand still, and its structure decays by default unless resources are spent to preserve it. They explain why maintenance, not initial development, dominates the lifecycle cost of long-lived systems, and why continual investment in reducing complexity is not optional overhead but the price of keeping a system usable. They gave software engineering a vocabulary for the inevitability of change decades before technical debt became a common term.

working.text: plan for an in-use system to require ongoing adaptation, since it degrades in usefulness if it stands still.
spend deliberate effort on refactoring and structure, because complexity rises on its own unless work is done to reduce it.
apply the laws to software embedded in a changing environment, not to self-contained programs judged only against a specification.

limits: The laws are empirical generalisations, not proven laws, and later studies, especially of open-source software, have qualified several. The Linux kernel's super-linear growth undermines the invariant-work-rate law and the growth slowdown for volunteer, distributed projects. Broad surveys find that typically only continuing change and continuing growth are confirmed across all systems, while the other six are violated by at least some projects, and applicability depends heavily on system type, measurement choices, and development model. The laws are also hard to falsify precisely, because terms like complexity, quality, and satisfaction lack universal operational definitions.
misreadings: They are not laws in the sense of physics but empirical observations about tendencies, with acknowledged exceptions. They do not apply to all software: they are explicitly scoped to E-type systems, and self-contained S-type programs are exempt. Increasing complexity is not inevitable and unstoppable; the second law says complexity rises unless work is done to reduce it, so refactoring is the built-in escape hatch. There have not always been eight laws; they grew from three to eight over two decades. And Lehman did not work alone: the early empirical foundation was a collaboration with Laszlo Belady.
origin: Developed by Meir 'Manny' Lehman with Laszlo Belady from studies of IBM's OS/360 begun in the late 1960s, first stated as three laws around 1974, set out canonically in Lehman's 1980 paper 'Programs, Life Cycles, and Laws of Software Evolution', and expanded to eight by the mid-1990s.

sources.text: Lehman, 'Programs, Life Cycles, and Laws of Software Evolution,' Proceedings of the IEEE 68(9) (1980): 1060-1076. — the laws and the S/P/E program classification.
Lehman's laws of software evolution, Wikipedia. — the eight laws, the E-type scope, and the open-source critiques.
